title: Road — Shared

rows.text: Road — Shared
102 draft packages. Images have no embedded text; wording listed as an overlay is rendered separately.
ENC-S01-A · Missing from the delivery

At a loading bay, a Spark driver reads the FTC’s Walmart settlement over allegedly misleading delivery-pay offers. Workers invite help reorganizing crates and offer spare lunch. The groceries arrived complete. The advertised earnings seem to have lost items in transit.
Help reorganize the crates → The lifting hurts, and matching every crate wears you down. You finish counting the goods; the pay dispute needs a different inventory.
Record the driver’s comparison → You record the driver’s offer and actual payment. The customer’s shopping list gets honored more accurately than the driver’s pay offer.
Accept some food for the road → You take the offered food. The driver checks the bag against the offer, delighted that lunch contains exactly what lunch promised.

Scene: A driver compares two blank phone screens while a loader indicates crates awaiting reorganization and unopened spare lunches. Two identical outlines of a delivery bag sit beside visibly unequal stacks of blank payment tokens.
Source: Walmart Agrees to $100 Million Judgment over Spark Driver Earnings Claims (2026-02-26)
Source: Walmart Fiscal 2026 Annual Report
ENC-S01-B · The engine has not read the waiver

EPA’s 2025 waiver changed summer E15 sales, not which vehicles can use it. A roadside parts clerk invites shelf-clearing help and offers leftover lunch. He puts the waiver beside an engine manual. Only one of these documents mentions what this engine actually needs.

Help clear the old display shelves → The work hurts your shoulders and wears you down. You separate sales notices from engine manuals before the paper authorizes another imaginary mechanical improvement.
Record the clerk’s comparison → You record the distinction and enjoy the clerk’s approval. A change in sale dates does not install a different engine.
Take some food from lunch → You take the offered food. The clerk promises no particular blend of enthusiasm will make it compatible with a fuel tank.

Scene: A clerk places a blank waiver and engine manual beside a stationary demonstration engine and uncleared shelves. The loose waiver is held over the engine like an attempted replacement part; the manual stays open beside the actual machinery.
Source: Ahead of Summer Driving Season, EPA Allows Nationwide Year-Round E15 (2025-04-28)
ENC-S01-C · The empty vault souvenir

Trump ordered a reserve of eligible government bitcoin. At a roadside coin swap, a dealer celebrates with souvenir vault boxes; the actual reserve holds digital assets. He invites help shifting stock and offers leftover supper. He has put two padlocks on an empty box.
Help shift the souvenir stock → The lifting hurts and the inventory wears you down. Every empty box receives careful handling; the cryptocurrency remains entirely elsewhere.
Record what the reserve actually holds → You record the digital-asset distinction and enjoy the dealer’s explanation. Neither padlock has managed to make the souvenir contain bitcoin.
Take some food from supper → You accept the offered food. The dealer opens its ordinary container with one hand, revealing the evening’s most immediately useful asset.
Scene: A dealer displays an open empty metal box with two padlocks and indicates unmoved stock beside unopened leftover supper. Two substantial padlocks protect a visibly empty souvenir vault.
Source: Establishment of the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and United States Digital Asset Stockpile (2025-03-06)
ENC-S02-A · Rent repaired by banner

The Justice Department proposed limits on RealPage’s use of competing landlords’ private data. A housing-promotion stall offers food for repeating ALL RENTS CAPPED. Its assistant wants supplies for a correction. The proposed settlement does not promise the price on that banner.
Donate supplies for the correction → Your supplies earn trust. The assistant replaces the promised universal cap with the actual proposed restrictions, losing several wonderfully misleading words.
Take the food; repeat all rents capped → You get food and lose credibility. Someone asks the promoter to honor the claim on a lease; he suddenly prefers the settlement’s details.
Use your paper; record the proposal → You preserve the proposal accurately and earn trust. The assistant circles court approval, a step the banner completed entirely on its own.

Scene: A promoter presents unopened food below a blank overstated banner while an assistant holds an unused correction sheet. A giant empty price-cap outline hangs above several much smaller blank lease forms.
Editable overlays: “ALL RENTS CAPPED” — Blank misleading banner
Source: Justice Department Requires RealPage to End Sharing Competitively Sensitive Information and Pricing Alignment (2025-11-24)
ENC-S02-B · Complimentary certainty

At a library health-information fair, volunteers need supplies to display the corrected MAHA citations. A wellness promoter offers your stopped crew some food for praising the original report as error-free. The volunteers have the corrections. The promoter has covered them with the biscuit tray.
Donate supplies for the correction display → You donate some supplies; volunteers record your help. The correction board rises above the biscuits. Evidence is finally operating at eye level.
Take the food; call it error-free → You take some food and praise the original report. The librarian corrects you. The promoter moves another biscuit over the missing study.
Use your paper; save the corrections → You use some supplies to save the original and corrected citations. The librarian moves the biscuit tray. The references immediately become easier to find.

Scene: A librarian holds a corrected-reference display beside a promoter's biscuit tray that obscures blank citation sheets; travelers consider the tables. A large biscuit tray physically covers the correction paperwork.
Editable overlays: “ERROR-FREE” — Blank promoter claim card
Source: May 2025 reporting identified nonexistent studies and other citation problems in the initial MAHA report. HHS said citation and…
ENC-S02-C · Search engine still present

A court barred Google’s exclusive search-distribution deals; it did not ban Google. At a refurbished-computer stall, the owner offers food to anyone repeating his GOOGLE BANNED pitch. His assistant wants supplies for an accurate comparison. The banned product is still open on every machine.
Donate supplies for the accurate comparison → Your supplies help the assistant explain the ruling, earning trust. The correction survives even with Google still visibly available.
Take the food; repeat Google banned → You get food and lose credibility. A visitor opens Google immediately, giving your announcement an unusually short shelf life.
Use your paper; record the distinction → You preserve the exclusivity distinction and earn trust. The owner discovers that removing a contract is harder to advertise than removing a website.

Scene: An owner offers an unopened lunch beside a blank provocative poster while the assistant indicates several blank laptop screens. The poster claims disappearance while identical search-box shapes remain on every screen; all wording is an overlay.
Editable overlays: “GOOGLE BANNED” — Blank pitch poster
Source: Justice Department Wins Significant Remedies Against Google (2025-09-02)
ENC-S03-A · Insufficient funds, additional funds required

Congress repealed the CFPB’s large-bank overdraft rule before its new pricing options took effect. At a café, the owner is collecting customer accounts and welcomes supplies for the effort. A negative balance has produced a positive business opportunity for the bank.
Read the worked fee example → The arithmetic wears you down. Every attempt to count the missing money has to make room for the charge for missing it.
Use some food; take a break → You eat and recover beside the café. Your lunch supplies shrink by exactly the amount of lunch you receive.
Donate supplies for collecting accounts → Your supplies help preserve the customers’ accounts and earn trust. The collection finally adds something without charging for the addition.
Scene: An owner arranges a small empty purse, blank receipt, and unused collection notebook beside an empty chair. A tiny empty purse is dwarfed by a long blank bank receipt curling across the table.
Source: Public Law 119-10: Disapproval of CFPB Overdraft Lending Rule (2025-05-09)
Source: CFPB: Closes Overdraft Loophole
ENC-S03-B · The yearly number and the hourly clock

A court vacated the planned federal overtime salary-threshold increase. At a roadside workers’ lunch, a clerk lays the abandoned increase beside her growing shift calendar. You can read, rest, or donate supplies. The boss likes the yearly salary number. He prefers fewer questions about the hours.
Study the shift-and-salary comparison → You count the hours until your head hurts. The yearly salary stays reassuringly still while the work keeps finding additional places to go.
Use some water; sit down → You drink and recover. For this little stretch of time, nobody is trying to fit another shift inside your existing paycheck.
Donate supplies to the workers’ table → Your supplies earn the workers’ trust. They extend the shift chart onto another sheet; the inconvenient hours have refused to fit the first one.
Scene: A clerk spreads a blank shift grid past the edge of a small salary card beside unused chairs. The shift grid runs off the table while the little salary card stays exactly the same size.
Source: DOL: Overtime Rulemaking (2024-11-15)
ENC-S03-C · The gift that needs a chair

Your aching crew stops at a temp-work briefing. The recruiter’s gift policy requires workers to document a free coffee while a news display covers the Pentagon’s Qatari jet. The coffee has its own folder. Applicants are still standing. A volunteer welcomes supply donations.
Read the gift-policy forms → You read until your head aches. The form asks how the coffee could influence you. Remaining conscious seems like a dangerous admission.
Use some food; sit outside → You use some food and recover on the outside bench. Your lunch comes from your own bag. The recruiter cannot find its foreign sponsor.

Donate supplies to the worker desk → You donate some supplies, and the worker volunteer records your help. The coffee’s folder gets a divider. Aircraft acceptance remains outside her stationery budget.

Scene: A recruiter displays a coffee folder beneath a blank jet-news panel while applicants and travelers stand near an unused outside bench. One coffee cup occupies a neatly arranged folder space while people have no indoor chairs.
Editable overlays: “PENTAGON ACCEPTED QATAR JET • MAY 2025” — Editable headline in blank news-display frame
Source: The Pentagon announced on May 21, 2025 that it had accepted a Boeing 747 from Qatar for presidential use. Acceptance prompted l…
ENC-S04-A · Three accents, no version of no

The FCC puts AI sales voices under robocall consent rules. At a dispatch-office rest stop, a worker tests a synthetic pitch that keeps changing accents when refused. She offers your crew a quiet corner. The voice has learned three accents and no version of no.
Read the call-consent explanation → You read until your head aches. The voice offers another accent; the missing permission remains exactly the same in all of them.
Use some food; rest outside → You eat and rest outside the speaker’s reach. The sales pitch continues improving its pronunciation of things nobody requested.
Ask the dispatcher for the quiet corner → She offers a resting spot and exchanges numbers. She asks before adding yours, a courtesy her expensive demonstration has yet to reproduce.

Scene: A dispatcher holds a plain speaker phone away from her ear and gestures toward an empty quiet alcove. Three differently shaped blank speech bubbles emerge from the same small speaker while the dispatcher maintains one clear stop gesture.
Source: FCC Makes AI-Generated Voices in Robocalls Illegal (2024-02-08)
ENC-S04-B · Proof of payment

At an airport-shuttle café, an attendant explains TSA’s $45 ConfirmID option for people without acceptable ID: payment does not guarantee verification. Your crew can rest here. The receipt can confidently establish that somebody is forty-five dollars poorer.
Read how ConfirmID works → The exceptions make your head spin. The receipt identifies the payment perfectly; the identity of the payer remains a separate question.
Use some food; rest by the van → You eat and rest beside the van. Nobody charges extra to confirm that the person enjoying the sandwich is you.
Ask the attendant for a quiet corner → The attendant offers a resting spot and exchanges contact details. Here, a recognizable face gets you a chair without an application fee.
Scene: An attendant holds a blank receipt beside a blank ID-shaped card and indicates an unused bench. The receipt is much larger than the card it cannot replace.
Editable overlays: “45 dollars” — Blank receipt total area
Source: Travelers Without REAL ID Could Pay $45 Fee for TSA’s ConfirmID Beginning February 1 (2026-02-01)
ENC-S04-C · A door with two instructions

Interior stopped Empire Wind construction in April 2025 and lifted the halt in May. A dockhand welcomes travelers at a roadside shelter with both notices. One rolled notice serves as a doorstop. The wind keeps slamming the door anyway. Even the shelter struggles to stay open.
Read the dated stop-and-restart notices → You read both notices until your head aches. The door shuts again, implementing the older instruction without waiting for the dockhand.
Use some food; rest in the shelter → You eat and rest in the shade. The dockhand settles the door with a boot, a remarkably short implementation process.
Ask the dockhand for a quiet spot → He offers a resting place and exchanges numbers. His shelter comes with one clear instruction: sit wherever the door cannot reach you.

Scene: A dockhand stands by a wind-blown door with a rolled old notice wedged inadequately beneath it; another blank notice is pinned to the wall beside empty seats. A flimsy rolled notice is being crushed beneath the much heavier swinging door it is supposed to hold open.
Source: BOEM: Empire Wind (2025-05-19)
Source: Empire Wind project updates
ENC-S05-A · Complete order, partial promise

The FTC and states settled allegations that Walmart’s Spark offers overstated driver earnings. At a pickup kiosk, a driver cooperative offers $10 to match offers with payments; food costs $6. The grocery order has substitutions. The drivers would prefer their wages without them.
Buy some food for $6 → You buy some food. The cooperative counts it into your bag exactly as advertised, giving the transaction an unexpectedly satisfying ending.
Match the delivery offers for $10 → You earn $10 and tired eyes. Every missing dollar gets its own line; none can be replaced with a different brand of dollar.
Pass on shopping and work → You leave annoyed. A driver checks the promised pay again, looking for the box where he supposedly agreed to substitutions.

Scene: A coordinator offers unmatched blank offer and payment cards beside complete grocery orders and unopened food for sale. A substitution divider stands between identical grocery bags and two visibly unequal piles of blank payment tokens.
Source: Walmart Agrees to $100 Million Judgment over Spark Driver Earnings Claims (2026-02-26)
Source: Walmart Fiscal 2026 Annual Report
ENC-S05-B · The complimentary evidence

A temp-work centre sells some food for $6 and offers your crew $10 to inventory gifts surrendered under its employer’s rule. Above the mint collection, a news screen reports the Pentagon’s Qatari jet. The recruiter has ordered a bigger evidence bag. For the mints.
Buy some food for $6 → You pay $6 and collect some food. Buying it avoids a gift declaration. The receipt is your lunch’s diplomatic passport.
Inventory the surrendered gifts for $10 → You earn $10 and a headache listing the mints. One is marked “possible influence, peppermint.” Nobody asks whether it needs a runway.
Pass on the food and job → You leave dispirited. The recruiter locks up a complimentary biscuit. The aircraft on the news remains complimentary.

Scene: A recruiter presents empty inventory sheets beside mints in oversized bags while travelers consider the posted food and job offers. A tiny collection of mints occupies enormous transparent evidence bags under a blank aircraft-news frame.
Editable overlays: “FOOD $6 • INVENTORY WORK $10 • PENTAGON ACCEPTED QATAR JET” — Editable copy split between blank offer board and blank news frame
Source: The Pentagon announced on May 21, 2025 that it had accepted a Boeing 747 from Qatar for presidential use. Acceptance prompted l…
ENC-S05-C · The final manufacturing step

After the FTC’s case against false Made in USA flag-product claims, a souvenir clerk checks supplier tags. Food costs $6; helping with the tags pays $10. A drawer is full of tiny flag stickers. Attaching one apparently was not the final stage of manufacturing.
Buy some food for $6 → You buy some food. The clerk leaves the flag stickers in their drawer, allowing lunch to make a modest claim about being lunch.
Check the supplier tags for $10 → You earn $10 and tired eyes. You match actual origins to tags; the decorative stickers contribute no manufacturing evidence.
Pass on the offer → You leave annoyed. The clerk closes the sticker drawer, retiring the shop’s smallest and least convincing domestic production line.

Scene: A clerk opens a drawer of unlettered flag-colored stickers beside unmatched blank supplier tags and unopened food. A tiny sticker applicator sits where a manufacturing tool might be, surrounded by already finished goods.
Source: FTC Announces Made in the USA Sweep (2026-04-14)
Source: Americana Liberty FTC case timeline: April 14, 2026
ENC-S06-A · Actual-size science

A library fair is checking the nonexistent studies from the initial MAHA report. The organizer offers your crew $8 to correct the display cards. The original author table has empty chairs. The corrected version needs actual people, which is proving a serious catering complication.
Check and save the citation history → You save the original and corrected references with a headache. The organizer cancels the imaginary seating plan. The room becomes smaller and more accurate.
Correct the display cards for $8 → You earn $8 and enjoy crossing out the fictional study. It is the first government-inspired job here completed without needing an imaginary qualification.
Leave the fair → You leave dispirited. The empty author chair has acquired a ribbon. The organizer still needs somebody who exists to move it.

Scene: An organizer displays blank cards awaiting correction beside empty author chairs while travelers consider the paid task. An elaborately reserved author chair has nobody to sit in it and a ceremonial ribbon on its back.
Editable overlays: “DISPLAY-CARD CORRECTIONS: $8” — Blank work-offer board
Source: May 2025 reporting identified nonexistent studies and other citation problems in the initial MAHA report. HHS said citation and…
ENC-S06-B · Choice, with arrows

A court restricted Google’s exclusive search-distribution deals in 2025. At a computer-recycling stall, a worker offers $8 to rearrange a demonstration board. It claims to show competing routes. Every arrow leads to the same search box, including the one labeled somewhere else.
Check and save what the ruling changed → You read the ruling until your eyes ache and keep the relevant pages. The worker finally moves the alternative arrow somewhere alternative.
Rearrange the demonstration arrows for $8 → You earn $8 and enjoy making a second route work. Choosing it no longer requires ignoring the directions supplied by the first company.
Skip the display → You leave annoyed. The worker follows every arrow once more and ends at the same box with impressive consistency.
Scene: A worker presents a blank board whose loose arrows all point toward one unlettered search-box shape. Even an arrow pointing away loops back to the same search box.
Editable overlays: “SOMEWHERE ELSE” — Separate editable label beside the looping arrow
Source: Justice Department Wins Significant Remedies Against Google (2025-09-02)
ENC-S06-C · Please add a person

The U.S. Copyright Office says prompting alone does not make someone an AI image’s author. At a sign stall, a painter offers $8 to arrange cutout letters while she redraws a client’s generated design. The supposedly unnecessary human is now the urgent order.

Check and save the authorship distinction → You preserve the human-contribution distinction through tired eyes. The client’s instruction to make it brilliant remains different from making it brilliant.
Arrange the cutout letters for $8 → You earn $8 and enjoy the work. The painter makes actual creative decisions while the client searches for a shortcut to those.
Leave the stall → You leave annoyed. The client tries adding please to the prompt, hoping courtesy will supply the missing authorship.

Scene: A painter holds a brush above an unfinished blank design while loose unlettered cutout shapes await arrangement. The client’s tiny prompt slip sits atop an enormous stack of rejected blank generated layouts.
Source: Copyright Office Releases Part 2 of Artificial Intelligence Report (2025-01-29)
ENC-S07-A · Strategic small change

A roadside coin dealer reads Trump’s order reserving eligible forfeited bitcoin instead of selling it. He declares his till a strategic reserve, then offers $12 to move a heavy cabinet. Supplies for the collectors’ lunch are welcome. Suddenly assets need legs.
Donate supplies for the collectors’ lunch → You share supplies and gain a contact. The dealer unlocks the snack cupboard, the only reserve with a sensible withdrawal policy.
Move the cabinet for $12 → You strain your shoulders and earn $12. His assets remain strategically stationary; your payment immediately starts planning a fuel purchase.
Pass on the request → You leave disappointed. The dealer studies the cabinet, hoping a holding strategy will eventually move it across the room.

Scene: The proprietor stands beside a locked till and an unmoved heavy display cabinet, offering a moving job. A tiny locked cash drawer receives a grand velvet cover while the bulky cabinet blocks its owner’s path.
Source: Establishment of the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and United States Digital Asset Stockpile (2025-03-06)
ENC-S07-B · Please confirm where headquarters is going

A court blocked the administration’s FBI headquarters move to the Reagan Building in August 2026. At a freight shop, a clerk has stopped labeling his spare office cabinet. Moving it pays $12; lunch supplies are welcome. He would like one address that survives the afternoon.
Donate supplies to the freight crew → You share supplies and gain a contact. The clerk puts lunch on the cabinet, confident that its destination is currently within reach.
Move the cabinet for $12 → You earn $12 and sore shoulders, enjoying a move that requires only the clerk’s agreement and a clear patch of floor.
Pass on the offer → You leave disappointed. The clerk keeps the address label loose, the cheapest infrastructure contingency he can manage.

Scene: A clerk holds an unattached blank address label beside a stationary office cabinet and offers a moving job. Two forwarding arrows point toward each other on a box perched atop the immobile cabinet.
Source: Maryland Attorney General Statement on FBI Headquarters Ruling (2026-08-17)
Source: AP reporting on court blocking FBI headquarters move
Source: FBI: New FBI Headquarters in Washington, DC
ENC-S07-C · Both ways at once

Trump wanted daylight saving ended, then urged more evening daylight in April 2025. A clock repairer offers $12 to move a cabinet and welcomes lunch supplies. He has put one presidential position on each face. The clock disagrees with itself.
Donate some food to the repairer → You share food and gain a contact. He sets a lunch timer, a tiny clock policy everyone can support.
Move the clock cabinet for $12 → You earn $12 and sore shoulders, laughing as the cabinet finally moves forward without requiring a position on summer time.
Pass on the offer → You leave irritated. The repairer points both hands upward and waits for Washington to decide which direction counts as progress.

Scene: A repairer points to the opposing faces of an unmoved two-faced clock cabinet and offers a moving job. The two faces of the same cabinet clock show different positions of the hands; no digits appear in the artwork.
Source: AP: Trump Calls for More Daylight as Debate over Clock Changes Continues (2025-04-11)
ENC-S08-A · The summer permission slip

A fuel clerk has kept EPA’s 2025 emergency waiver allowing summer E15 sales. He invites you to inspect its temporary dates while selling some food for $5. The blend stayed the same. Its permission to exist beside a summer picnic required renewal.
Check and save the waiver’s limits → You save the temporary dates through tired eyes. The federal paperwork changes seasons more often than the fuel changes ingredients.
Buy some food for $5 → You buy some food. The clerk hands it over without requesting an emergency waiver for eating lunch during summer.
Skip the food and waiver → You leave annoyed. The clerk folds the expired notice beside the pump cover, two different ways of putting the same fuel away.
Scene: A clerk holds a saved blank waiver beside a rolled pump cover and unopened food for sale. A pump cover has a tiny calendar pinned to it like a garment waiting for its approved season.
Editable overlays: “2025 TEMPORARY E15 WAIVER” — Blank saved notice header
Source: Ahead of Summer Driving Season, EPA Allows Nationwide Year-Round E15 (2025-04-28)
ENC-S08-B · A face accepted by the sandwich counter

TSA charges $45 for a ConfirmID attempt when travelers lack acceptable identification. At an airport-access grocery, the clerk sells some food for $5 and invites a comparison of the rules. She does not know your name. This has not prevented her from locating lunch.
Check and save the identification rules → You save the ID list, eyes aching. The clerk recognizes a need for lunch without first charging $45 to investigate it.
Buy some food for $5 → You buy food. Your money works, and the clerk lets the sandwich travel with you without attempting to verify either of you.
Leave without reading or eating → You leave annoyed. The clerk puts the sandwich back, still completely certain where it is despite never having checked its documents.

Scene: A clerk presents unopened food beside a blank accepted-ID notice and an ordinary till. A plain wrapped sandwich rests confidently on the counter beside a much fussier arrangement of blank identity-card examples.
Source: Travelers Without REAL ID Could Pay $45 Fee for TSA’s ConfirmID Beginning February 1 (2026-02-01)
ENC-S08-C · Buy another box

California now separates quality-date wording from safety-date wording on covered new foods. At a grocery, a clerk offers food for $5 and invites you to check a supplier’s examples. The supplier’s preferred date instruction is BUY ANOTHER BOX.
Check and save the date distinctions → You preserve the quality-and-safety distinction through tired eyes. The supplier’s preferred instruction turns out to describe a sales target, not a date.
Buy some food for $5 → You buy food. The clerk gives you one box rather than implementing the supplier’s entire long-term relationship with your wallet.
Pass on the examples and food → You leave annoyed. The clerk sets the supplier’s preferred label beside the till, where its actual purpose requires less explanation.
Scene: A clerk presents blank supplier examples beside unopened food and an unused till. One blank date card is disproportionately large and shaped like a second shopping box.
Editable overlays: “BUY ANOTHER BOX” — Blank supplier example card
Source: California AB 660: Food and Beverage Date Labeling (2026-07-01)
Source: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Food Date Labeling
ENC-S09-A · Patriotically air-conditioned

Florida barred local heat-break rules. At a roadside trade fair, a contractor wants the same freedom here. He praises toughness from inside a refrigerated sales trailer. A worker points you toward shade; the trailer’s exhaust is blowing directly onto her.
Rest in shade; share food → Food and shade restore you. The contractor shuts his trailer window to explain more comfortably why workers need fewer protections.
Praise the freedom to endure → His certainty calms you. You repeat it; the worker offers to swap places with his air conditioner. Your authority evaporates.
Skip the fair → You leave irritated. The contractor puts on a cardigan before recording another message about people becoming too sensitive to heat.

Scene: The contractor gestures from a cooled trailer while the worker indicates an unoccupied shaded rest area. Trailer exhaust blows across the worker while a cardigan hangs inside the cooled office.
Editable overlays: “COPY FLORIDA: FEWER HEAT RULES” — Blank trade-fair placard
Source: DeSantis signed Florida 2024 law barring local government heat/water-break mandates. This does not make drinking water illegal …
ENC-S09-B · The research was feeling shy

The MAHA report cited studies that did not exist. You stop at a wellness fair where a vendor says missing evidence proves how suppressed it is. A first-aid volunteer offers a shaded seat. The vendor’s certificate has been printed backwards for additional secrecy.
Rest; use some supplies → You eat and recover in the shade. The volunteer reads the backwards certificate in a mirror; it remains impressively unqualified.
Agree the missing studies prove it → The neat explanation settles your nerves. A visitor asks whether an empty bottle therefore contains the strongest possible medicine.
Leave the fair → You leave disappointed. The vendor covers the blank reference list, protecting the authorities from discovering absolutely nothing.
Scene: The vendor displays a blank reverse-facing certificate while a volunteer offers an empty shaded chair. The secretive certificate has no readable evidence on either side.
Editable overlays: “EVIDENCE TOO SUPPRESSED TO DISPLAY” — Editable caption beside blank certificate
Source: May 2025 reporting identified nonexistent studies and other citation errors in the MAHA report; corrected versions followed. Do…
ENC-S09-C · Wealth you cannot eat

At a collectors’ roadside picnic, a dealer celebrates Trump’s order retaining eligible forfeited bitcoin in a federal reserve. His own lunch money is locked in a display case as a joke. You can rest here. He calls the empty plate asset preservation.
Rest in shade; share some food → You share food and recover. The dealer unlocks his lunch money, briefly abandoning the strategic objective of watching it remain money.
Agree every locked asset is usable wealth → The neat explanation comforts you until someone asks you to buy lunch with the display. Your confidence loses an important qualification.
Pass on the picnic → You leave disappointed. The dealer admires the preserved money while the empty plate achieves another excellent quarter without depreciation.

Scene: A dealer gestures proudly toward money-shaped blank tokens inside a locked case beside an empty plate. The display case is comfortably full while the plate directly beneath it is completely empty.
Source: Establishment of the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and United States Digital Asset Stockpile (2025-03-06)
ENC-S10-A · Permanent paint, temporary destination

A court blocked the administration’s FBI headquarters move to the Reagan Building in August 2026. A roadside map seller offers $7 to correct a display arrow. He used permanent paint for the original announcement. Washington has been less committed to the address.
Correct the display arrow for $7 → You earn $7 and tired eyes. The arrow now acknowledges the court decision, an expensive qualification to add in permanent paint.
Post the actual dated correction → You post the correction and earn trust. The seller finally separates an announced destination from somewhere the moving van can safely be sent.
Skip the job → You leave annoyed. The seller considers a removable arrow, bringing his map technology up to the level of the government’s real-estate certainty.
Scene: A seller holds an unopened paint tin beside a fixed blank arrow and an unattached correction panel. A heavy permanent arrow is surrounded by tiny removable arrows suggesting several revisions.
Source: Maryland Attorney General Statement on FBI Headquarters Ruling (2026-08-17)
Source: AP reporting on court blocking FBI headquarters move
Source: FBI: New FBI Headquarters in Washington, DC
ENC-S10-B · The extra cleaning hour

Trump urged more evening daylight in April 2025. A motel manager misunderstood and printed LONGER DAYS, then scheduled an extra cleaning round in the supposed new hour. His clerk offers $7 to correct the labels. Neither Congress nor the clocks supplied another hour of labor.
Replace the mistaken labels for $7 → You earn $7 and tired eyes. The day returns to its usual length, leaving the manager to find a real person for his extra round.
Show what changing the clocks actually does → You demonstrate the shifted clock and earn trust. The clerk crosses out a cleaning round that existed entirely inside the manager’s interpretation.
Leave the labels alone → You leave annoyed. The manager rotates the clock face, trying one last inexpensive way to add staff time.

Scene: A clerk offers untouched replacement cards while the manager points at a normal blank-faced clock beside a crowded shift grid. One extra blank shift block protrudes beyond the edge of an otherwise complete circular clock display.
Editable overlays: “LONGER DAYS” — Blank mistaken promotional card
Source: AP: Trump Calls for More Daylight as Debate over Clock Changes Continues (2025-04-11)
ENC-S10-C · The prompt-signing ceremony

The U.S. Copyright Office says prompts alone do not establish authorship of AI output. A roadside portrait seller offers $7 to replace misleading ownership cards. His customer has already signed the prompt in gold ink. The machine has not become more human in response.
Replace the misleading cards for $7 → You earn $7 and tired eyes. The new cards stop promising that an elaborate signature settles the authorship question.
Point out the actual human contributions → You distinguish human creative work from prompting and earn trust. Gold ink remains excellent for signatures and less useful for creating missing artwork.
Skip the job → You leave annoyed. The customer adds a flourish beneath the prompt, increasing the signature’s area without changing who made the image.

Scene: A seller offers unprocessed ownership cards while a customer holds a gold pen above a blank prompt slip. The ornate gold flourish on the prompt slip is much larger than the small blank image being discussed; no actual lettering is embedded.
Source: Copyright Office Releases Part 2 of Artificial Intelligence Report (2025-01-29)
ENC-S11-A · Executive sandwich duties

At a lunch counter, a worker shows you the court decision that killed the planned federal overtime-threshold increase. The boss has supplied a managerial badge instead. She offers $9 to match timecards and welcomes company over lunch. The badge works overtime.
Share some food with the worker → You share lunch, laugh, and exchange numbers. She removes the managerial badge; the sandwich tastes equally senior without it.
Match the timecards for $9 → You earn $9 and her endorsement through tired eyes. The cards count hours; the badge contributes an impressive job title.
Get back on the road → You leave annoyed. The worker pins the badge to a chair during her break. Management is finally sitting through a whole shift.
Scene: A worker displays a blank grandiose badge above unprocessed timecards and an unopened lunch. The oversized badge nearly covers an ordinary apron pocket.
Source: DOL: Overtime Rulemaking (2024-11-15)
ENC-S11-B · The library needs a patriotic eraser

Trump’s patriotic-education order reaches a community book sale. The organizer offers $9 to sort donated books. A campaigner wants every unpleasant chapter removed from the history section. The thickest book is beginning to resemble a coaster.

Sort the labels for $10 → Ten dollars and a headache. The technician retrieves another page from the hedge; wind continues producing results without waiting for the speech to finish.
Record the technician’s account → You gain evidence and a contact, mentally tired. He distinguishes paused approvals from moving air, a distinction the flying order demonstrates repeatedly.
Keep moving → You leave the offer behind. A speaker asks someone to hold the paperwork still while he explains the advantages of stopping wind development.
Scene: The technician offers unsorted labels while loose order pages lift in the breeze. The order opposing new wind development cannot remain on the table without assistance.
Editable overlays: “WIND APPROVAL PAUSE” — Editable order heading

ENC-S32-B · The unreliable panel is doing the work

Trump ordered strict enforcement of wind and solar tax-credit terminations, calling those sources unreliable. At a repair fair, a technician offers $10 to sort component labels. The anti-solar presentation is powered by the small solar panel nobody wants included in the photograph.
Sort the labels for $10 → Ten dollars and aching eyes. The panel powers another slide explaining its unreliability; the technician asks whether it should stop interrupting the argument.
Save the setup and technician’s account → You gain evidence and a contact through a headache. The presentation’s most reliable participant is the one being accused on every slide.
Continue the trip → You leave the offer behind. The photographer moves the panel out of frame, successfully reducing visible solar dependence without reducing solar dependence.
Scene: The technician offers component labels while a cable visibly connects a panel to the presentation screen. The accused energy source is powering the accusation.
Editable overlays: “UNRELIABLE ENERGY” — Editable slide heading
Source: July 2025 order directed strict enforcement of the 2025 law’s termination of specified wind and solar tax credits. Unreliable a…
ENC-S32-C · An actual choice

After a court restricted Google’s exclusive distribution deals, a computer refurbisher makes a demonstration keyboard with several search keys. Sorting spare keycaps pays $10; he also invites you to check the ruling. Previously, his display offered four choices of the same button.
Sort the spare keycaps for $10 → You earn $10 and tired eyes. The refurbished keyboard can finally suggest that a choice might lead somewhere different.

Record the ruling with the refurbisher → You save the exclusivity distinction, mentally tired, and gain a contact. He keeps Google available; the demonstration needs competition, not a disappearance trick.
Keep moving → You leave the stall. The refurbisher tests a second search key and enjoys its modest refusal to be the first one.

Scene: A refurbisher presents an unfinished keyboard beside loose unlettered keycaps and a blank ruling summary. Four identical oversized keys sit beside one ordinary spare key in a contrasting color, with no embedded lettering.
Source: Justice Department Wins Significant Remedies Against Google (2025-09-02)
ENC-S33-A · The tank has run out of freedom

Trump ordered showerhead deregulation. At a desert service stop, a celebratory display is draining the tank. The plumber offers water for help shutting it off or $12 for the heavier work. The owner asks whether the empty tank is refusing to cooperate politically.
Help shut it off; take water → You gain water and some peace of mind. The plumber demonstrates the off switch, a technology omitted from the freedom ceremony.
Do the heavier work for $12 → Twelve dollars and sore muscles. You haul the equipment while the owner asks whether refilling the tank counts as government interference.
Keep driving → You leave the offer behind. The display coughs; the owner checks the banner instead of the water level.
Scene: The plumber offers help options while water drains from a display toward a low tank. The owner inspects a freedom banner instead of the visibly low water supply.
Editable overlays: “SHOWER FREEDOM” — Editable banner
Source: April 2025 Executive Order 14264 directed rescission of the 2021 showerhead definition; it framed the action as restoring freed…
ENC-S33-B · A nationally protected blockage

Trump ordered federal agencies back to plastic straws. At a desert drinks promotion, the giant ceremonial straw blocks the refill station. The installer offers water for clearing the walkway or $12 to move its heavy base. The straw has secured access to all the drinks.
Clear the walkway; take water → You gain water and clear your head. Ordinary people can reach the tap once the national drinking priority moves out of their way.
Move the base for $12 → Twelve dollars and aching muscles. You carry the object designed to prove that drinking ought to require less effort.
Continue the trip → You leave the offer behind. The installer bends the giant straw sideways, achieving the national strategy’s first practical compromise with thirst.
Scene: The installer offers help options beside a giant straw sculpture blocking access. The drinking implement prevents people reaching drinking water.
Editable overlays: “BACK TO PLASTIC” — Editable promotion heading
Source: February 2025 order directed agencies to end paper-straw procurement and develop a broader strategy. It did not prohibit custom…
ENC-S33-C · The inspection left a forwarding fee

Texas ended most noncommercial safety inspections but kept a $7.50 inspection-program replacement fee. At a Texas garage, the mechanic offers water for clearing access or $12 to shift barriers. The inspection bay is empty. Its fee has kept the appointment.
Clear access; take some water → You clear the approach, collect water, and enjoy a useful result. The empty inspection bay contributes no further inspection to the arrangement.
Move the barriers for $12 → You earn $12 and sore muscles. The barriers move on; the replacement fee has secured a more permanent position.
Keep moving → You leave the garage. The mechanic checks the empty bay once more, just in case the fee has grown an inspector.

Scene: A mechanic indicates barriers awaiting relocation and unopened drinking water beside an empty inspection bay. A small blank fee notice occupies the prominent position where inspection equipment once stood.
Editable overlays: “7.50 dollars replacement fee” — Blank notice at bay entrance
Source: Texas DPS: Vehicle Safety Inspection Changes Take Effect January 2025 (undated)
ENC-S34-A · A fee for the lack of money

Congress repealed the CFPB’s new overdraft rule for very large banks. At a roadside payroll kiosk, a clerk offers $16 to match account notices and invites a closer comparison. The charge is easiest to describe when the customer can least afford the description.
Match the account notices for $16 → You earn $16 and tired eyes. The account receives a charge for running short, then has to run shorter to cover it.
Compare the repeal with the old options → You read until your eyes ache. Charging someone for having no money remains a remarkably confident business model.
Keep moving → You leave the kiosk. Its empty coin dish remains the most accurate illustration of the customer account.
Scene: A clerk offers unmatched blank account notices beside a shallow empty coin dish. A long blank fee receipt spirals into an empty coin dish without adding anything to it.

Source: CFPB: Closes Overdraft Loophole
ENC-S34-B · Ten fewer ways to fold

Trump told agencies to identify ten rules to scrap for each new one. A hotel owner is copying him: one new towel rule has cost him ten folding instructions. He offers $16 to sort linen labels. His fitted sheet has captured one arm. Deregulation is reaching for the other.
Sort linen labels for $16 → You earn $16 and rest your aching eyes. The sorted tags say FITTED. The owner asks whether you could repeal that part too.

Compare his claim with the old instructions → You save his boast, the order and both instruction cards, head aching. One new rule removed ten useful steps. The sheet now contains less regulation and one whole owner.
Keep moving → You leave the offer behind. He announces that he has eliminated red tape. The elastic captures his other arm.

Scene: The worker indicates the unsorted labels while the owner holds up an altered folding chart with his free hand; travelers consider the job. The man celebrating fewer instructions is trapped inside the object those instructions explained.

ENC-S34-C · Tomorrow’s investor needs today’s invoice

Trump Accounts offer eligible newborns $1,000 unavailable for childhood bills. At a baby-goods warehouse, $16 is offered to sort delivery labels. A parent compares the account announcement with a diaper invoice. The baby has begun rejecting delayed gratification at full volume.
Sort delivery labels for $16 → Sixteen dollars and a headache. The diaper boxes leave today; the money meant to celebrate the baby’s future remains admirably patient.
Compare the account rules with the invoice → You save the mismatch through aching eyes. The parent asks whether the diapers might accept a payment schedule based on adulthood.
Keep moving → You leave the job behind. The baby grabs the announcement, becoming the first person here to extract immediate practical entertainment from it.
Scene: The dispatcher offers unsorted labels while the parent compares an account notice with an immediate invoice. A long-term investment notice is held beside urgent diaper deliveries.
Editable overlays: “$1,000 FOR THE FUTURE” — Editable announcement heading; “DUE NOW” — Editable fictional invoice stamp

ENC-S01-A · Missing from the delivery
At a loading bay, a Spark driver reads the FTC’s Walmart settlement over allegedly misleading delivery-pay offers. Workers invite help reorganizing crates and offer spare lunch. The groceries arrived complete. The advertised earnings seem to have lost items in transit.
Help reorganize the crates → The lifting hurts, and matching every crate wears you down. You finish counting the goods; the pay dispute needs a different inventory.
Record the driver’s comparison → You record the driver’s offer and actual payment. The customer’s shopping list gets honored more accurately than the driver’s pay offer.
Accept some food for the road → You take the offered food. The driver checks the bag against the offer, delighted that lunch contains exactly what lunch promised.
Scene: A driver compares two blank phone screens while a loader indicates crates awaiting reorganization and unopened spare lunches. Two identical outlines of a delivery bag sit beside visibly unequal stacks of blank payment tokens.
Source: Walmart Agrees to $100 Million Judgment over Spark Driver Earnings Claims (2026-02-26)
Source: Walmart Fiscal 2026 Annual Report
ENC-S01-B · The engine has not read the waiver
EPA’s 2025 waiver changed summer E15 sales, not which vehicles can use it. A roadside parts clerk invites shelf-clearing help and offers leftover lunch. He puts the waiver beside an engine manual. Only one of these documents mentions what this engine actually needs.
Help clear the old display shelves → The work hurts your shoulders and wears you down. You separate sales notices from engine manuals before the paper authorizes another imaginary mechanical improvement.
Record the clerk’s comparison → You record the distinction and enjoy the clerk’s approval. A change in sale dates does not install a different engine.
Take some food from lunch → You take the offered food. The clerk promises no particular blend of enthusiasm will make it compatible with a fuel tank.
Scene: A clerk places a blank waiver and engine manual beside a stationary demonstration engine and uncleared shelves. The loose waiver is held over the engine like an attempted replacement part; the manual stays open beside the actual machinery.
Source: Ahead of Summer Driving Season, EPA Allows Nationwide Year-Round E15 (2025-04-28)
ENC-S01-C · The empty vault souvenir
Trump ordered a reserve of eligible government bitcoin. At a roadside coin swap, a dealer celebrates with souvenir vault boxes; the actual reserve holds digital assets. He invites help shifting stock and offers leftover supper. He has put two padlocks on an empty box.
Help shift the souvenir stock → The lifting hurts and the inventory wears you down. Every empty box receives careful handling; the cryptocurrency remains entirely elsewhere.
Record what the reserve actually holds → You record the digital-asset distinction and enjoy the dealer’s explanation. Neither padlock has managed to make the souvenir contain bitcoin.
Take some food from supper → You accept the offered food. The dealer opens its ordinary container with one hand, revealing the evening’s most immediately useful asset.
Scene: A dealer displays an open empty metal box with two padlocks and indicates unmoved stock beside unopened leftover supper. Two substantial padlocks protect a visibly empty souvenir vault.
Source: Establishment of the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and United States Digital Asset Stockpile (2025-03-06)
ENC-S02-A · Rent repaired by banner
The Justice Department proposed limits on RealPage’s use of competing landlords’ private data. A housing-promotion stall offers food for repeating ALL RENTS CAPPED. Its assistant wants supplies for a correction. The proposed settlement does not promise the price on that banner.
Donate supplies for the correction → Your supplies earn trust. The assistant replaces the promised universal cap with the actual proposed restrictions, losing several wonderfully misleading words.
Take the food; repeat all rents capped → You get food and lose credibility. Someone asks the promoter to honor the claim on a lease; he suddenly prefers the settlement’s details.
Use your paper; record the proposal → You preserve the proposal accurately and earn trust. The assistant circles court approval, a step the banner completed entirely on its own.
Scene: A promoter presents unopened food below a blank overstated banner while an assistant holds an unused correction sheet. A giant empty price-cap outline hangs above several much smaller blank lease forms.
Editable overlays: “ALL RENTS CAPPED” — Blank misleading banner
Source: Justice Department Requires RealPage to End Sharing Competitively Sensitive Information and Pricing Alignment (2025-11-24)
ENC-S02-B · Complimentary certainty
At a library health-information fair, volunteers need supplies to display the corrected MAHA citations. A wellness promoter offers your stopped crew some food for praising the original report as error-free. The volunteers have the corrections. The promoter has covered them with the biscuit tray.
Donate supplies for the correction display → You donate some supplies; volunteers record your help. The correction board rises above the biscuits. Evidence is finally operating at eye level.
Take the food; call it error-free → You take some food and praise the original report. The librarian corrects you. The promoter moves another biscuit over the missing study.
Use your paper; save the corrections → You use some supplies to save the original and corrected citations. The librarian moves the biscuit tray. The references immediately become easier to find.
Scene: A librarian holds a corrected-reference display beside a promoter's biscuit tray that obscures blank citation sheets; travelers consider the tables. A large biscuit tray physically covers the correction paperwork.
Editable overlays: “ERROR-FREE” — Blank promoter claim card
Source: May 2025 reporting identified nonexistent studies and other citation problems in the initial MAHA report. HHS said citation and…
ENC-S02-C · Search engine still present
A court barred Google’s exclusive search-distribution deals; it did not ban Google. At a refurbished-computer stall, the owner offers food to anyone repeating his GOOGLE BANNED pitch. His assistant wants supplies for an accurate comparison. The banned product is still open on every machine.
Donate supplies for the accurate comparison → Your supplies help the assistant explain the ruling, earning trust. The correction survives even with Google still visibly available.
Take the food; repeat Google banned → You get food and lose credibility. A visitor opens Google immediately, giving your announcement an unusually short shelf life.
Use your paper; record the distinction → You preserve the exclusivity distinction and earn trust. The owner discovers that removing a contract is harder to advertise than removing a website.
Scene: An owner offers an unopened lunch beside a blank provocative poster while the assistant indicates several blank laptop screens. The poster claims disappearance while identical search-box shapes remain on every screen; all wording is an overlay.
Editable overlays: “GOOGLE BANNED” — Blank pitch poster
Source: Justice Department Wins Significant Remedies Against Google (2025-09-02)
ENC-S03-A · Insufficient funds, additional funds required
Congress repealed the CFPB’s large-bank overdraft rule before its new pricing options took effect. At a café, the owner is collecting customer accounts and welcomes supplies for the effort. A negative balance has produced a positive business opportunity for the bank.
Read the worked fee example → The arithmetic wears you down. Every attempt to count the missing money has to make room for the charge for missing it.
Use some food; take a break → You eat and recover beside the café. Your lunch supplies shrink by exactly the amount of lunch you receive.
Donate supplies for collecting accounts → Your supplies help preserve the customers’ accounts and earn trust. The collection finally adds something without charging for the addition.
Scene: An owner arranges a small empty purse, blank receipt, and unused collection notebook beside an empty chair. A tiny empty purse is dwarfed by a long blank bank receipt curling across the table.
Source: Public Law 119-10: Disapproval of CFPB Overdraft Lending Rule (2025-05-09)
Source: CFPB: Closes Overdraft Loophole
ENC-S03-B · The yearly number and the hourly clock
A court vacated the planned federal overtime salary-threshold increase. At a roadside workers’ lunch, a clerk lays the abandoned increase beside her growing shift calendar. You can read, rest, or donate supplies. The boss likes the yearly salary number. He prefers fewer questions about the hours.
Study the shift-and-salary comparison → You count the hours until your head hurts. The yearly salary stays reassuringly still while the work keeps finding additional places to go.
Use some water; sit down → You drink and recover. For this little stretch of time, nobody is trying to fit another shift inside your existing paycheck.
Donate supplies to the workers’ table → Your supplies earn the workers’ trust. They extend the shift chart onto another sheet; the inconvenient hours have refused to fit the first one.
Scene: A clerk spreads a blank shift grid past the edge of a small salary card beside unused chairs. The shift grid runs off the table while the little salary card stays exactly the same size.
Source: DOL: Overtime Rulemaking (2024-11-15)
ENC-S03-C · The gift that needs a chair
Your aching crew stops at a temp-work briefing. The recruiter’s gift policy requires workers to document a free coffee while a news display covers the Pentagon’s Qatari jet. The coffee has its own folder. Applicants are still standing. A volunteer welcomes supply donations.
Read the gift-policy forms → You read until your head aches. The form asks how the coffee could influence you. Remaining conscious seems like a dangerous admission.
Use some food; sit outside → You use some food and recover on the outside bench. Your lunch comes from your own bag. The recruiter cannot find its foreign sponsor.
Donate supplies to the worker desk → You donate some supplies, and the worker volunteer records your help. The coffee’s folder gets a divider. Aircraft acceptance remains outside her stationery budget.
Scene: A recruiter displays a coffee folder beneath a blank jet-news panel while applicants and travelers stand near an unused outside bench. One coffee cup occupies a neatly arranged folder space while people have no indoor chairs.
Editable overlays: “PENTAGON ACCEPTED QATAR JET • MAY 2025” — Editable headline in blank news-display frame
Source: The Pentagon announced on May 21, 2025 that it had accepted a Boeing 747 from Qatar for presidential use. Acceptance prompted l…
ENC-S04-A · Three accents, no version of no
The FCC puts AI sales voices under robocall consent rules. At a dispatch-office rest stop, a worker tests a synthetic pitch that keeps changing accents when refused. She offers your crew a quiet corner. The voice has learned three accents and no version of no.
Read the call-consent explanation → You read until your head aches. The voice offers another accent; the missing permission remains exactly the same in all of them.
Use some food; rest outside → You eat and rest outside the speaker’s reach. The sales pitch continues improving its pronunciation of things nobody requested.
Ask the dispatcher for the quiet corner → She offers a resting spot and exchanges numbers. She asks before adding yours, a courtesy her expensive demonstration has yet to reproduce.
Scene: A dispatcher holds a plain speaker phone away from her ear and gestures toward an empty quiet alcove. Three differently shaped blank speech bubbles emerge from the same small speaker while the dispatcher maintains one clear stop gesture.
Source: FCC Makes AI-Generated Voices in Robocalls Illegal (2024-02-08)
ENC-S04-B · Proof of payment
At an airport-shuttle café, an attendant explains TSA’s $45 ConfirmID option for people without acceptable ID: payment does not guarantee verification. Your crew can rest here. The receipt can confidently establish that somebody is forty-five dollars poorer.
Read how ConfirmID works → The exceptions make your head spin. The receipt identifies the payment perfectly; the identity of the payer remains a separate question.
Use some food; rest by the van → You eat and rest beside the van. Nobody charges extra to confirm that the person enjoying the sandwich is you.
Ask the attendant for a quiet corner → The attendant offers a resting spot and exchanges contact details. Here, a recognizable face gets you a chair without an application fee.
Scene: An attendant holds a blank receipt beside a blank ID-shaped card and indicates an unused bench. The receipt is much larger than the card it cannot replace.
Editable overlays: “45 dollars” — Blank receipt total area
Source: Travelers Without REAL ID Could Pay $45 Fee for TSA’s ConfirmID Beginning February 1 (2026-02-01)
ENC-S04-C · A door with two instructions
Interior stopped Empire Wind construction in April 2025 and lifted the halt in May. A dockhand welcomes travelers at a roadside shelter with both notices. One rolled notice serves as a doorstop. The wind keeps slamming the door anyway. Even the shelter struggles to stay open.
Read the dated stop-and-restart notices → You read both notices until your head aches. The door shuts again, implementing the older instruction without waiting for the dockhand.
Use some food; rest in the shelter → You eat and rest in the shade. The dockhand settles the door with a boot, a remarkably short implementation process.
Ask the dockhand for a quiet spot → He offers a resting place and exchanges numbers. His shelter comes with one clear instruction: sit wherever the door cannot reach you.
Scene: A dockhand stands by a wind-blown door with a rolled old notice wedged inadequately beneath it; another blank notice is pinned to the wall beside empty seats. A flimsy rolled notice is being crushed beneath the much heavier swinging door it is supposed to hold open.
Source: BOEM: Empire Wind (2025-05-19)
Source: Empire Wind project updates
ENC-S05-A · Complete order, partial promise
The FTC and states settled allegations that Walmart’s Spark offers overstated driver earnings. At a pickup kiosk, a driver cooperative offers $10 to match offers with payments; food costs $6. The grocery order has substitutions. The drivers would prefer their wages without them.
Buy some food for $6 → You buy some food. The cooperative counts it into your bag exactly as advertised, giving the transaction an unexpectedly satisfying ending.
Match the delivery offers for $10 → You earn $10 and tired eyes. Every missing dollar gets its own line; none can be replaced with a different brand of dollar.
Pass on shopping and work → You leave annoyed. A driver checks the promised pay again, looking for the box where he supposedly agreed to substitutions.
Scene: A coordinator offers unmatched blank offer and payment cards beside complete grocery orders and unopened food for sale. A substitution divider stands between identical grocery bags and two visibly unequal piles of blank payment tokens.
Source: Walmart Agrees to $100 Million Judgment over Spark Driver Earnings Claims (2026-02-26)
Source: Walmart Fiscal 2026 Annual Report
ENC-S05-B · The complimentary evidence
A temp-work centre sells some food for $6 and offers your crew $10 to inventory gifts surrendered under its employer’s rule. Above the mint collection, a news screen reports the Pentagon’s Qatari jet. The recruiter has ordered a bigger evidence bag. For the mints.
Buy some food for $6 → You pay $6 and collect some food. Buying it avoids a gift declaration. The receipt is your lunch’s diplomatic passport.
Inventory the surrendered gifts for $10 → You earn $10 and a headache listing the mints. One is marked “possible influence, peppermint.” Nobody asks whether it needs a runway.
Pass on the food and job → You leave dispirited. The recruiter locks up a complimentary biscuit. The aircraft on the news remains complimentary.
Scene: A recruiter presents empty inventory sheets beside mints in oversized bags while travelers consider the posted food and job offers. A tiny collection of mints occupies enormous transparent evidence bags under a blank aircraft-news frame.
Editable overlays: “FOOD $6 • INVENTORY WORK $10 • PENTAGON ACCEPTED QATAR JET” — Editable copy split between blank offer board and blank news frame
Source: The Pentagon announced on May 21, 2025 that it had accepted a Boeing 747 from Qatar for presidential use. Acceptance prompted l…
ENC-S05-C · The final manufacturing step
After the FTC’s case against false Made in USA flag-product claims, a souvenir clerk checks supplier tags. Food costs $6; helping with the tags pays $10. A drawer is full of tiny flag stickers. Attaching one apparently was not the final stage of manufacturing.
Buy some food for $6 → You buy some food. The clerk leaves the flag stickers in their drawer, allowing lunch to make a modest claim about being lunch.
Check the supplier tags for $10 → You earn $10 and tired eyes. You match actual origins to tags; the decorative stickers contribute no manufacturing evidence.
Pass on the offer → You leave annoyed. The clerk closes the sticker drawer, retiring the shop’s smallest and least convincing domestic production line.
Scene: A clerk opens a drawer of unlettered flag-colored stickers beside unmatched blank supplier tags and unopened food. A tiny sticker applicator sits where a manufacturing tool might be, surrounded by already finished goods.
Source: FTC Announces Made in the USA Sweep (2026-04-14)
Source: Americana Liberty FTC case timeline: April 14, 2026
ENC-S06-A · Actual-size science
A library fair is checking the nonexistent studies from the initial MAHA report. The organizer offers your crew $8 to correct the display cards. The original author table has empty chairs. The corrected version needs actual people, which is proving a serious catering complication.
Check and save the citation history → You save the original and corrected references with a headache. The organizer cancels the imaginary seating plan. The room becomes smaller and more accurate.
Correct the display cards for $8 → You earn $8 and enjoy crossing out the fictional study. It is the first government-inspired job here completed without needing an imaginary qualification.
Leave the fair → You leave dispirited. The empty author chair has acquired a ribbon. The organizer still needs somebody who exists to move it.
Scene: An organizer displays blank cards awaiting correction beside empty author chairs while travelers consider the paid task. An elaborately reserved author chair has nobody to sit in it and a ceremonial ribbon on its back.
Editable overlays: “DISPLAY-CARD CORRECTIONS: $8” — Blank work-offer board
Source: May 2025 reporting identified nonexistent studies and other citation problems in the initial MAHA report. HHS said citation and…
ENC-S06-B · Choice, with arrows
A court restricted Google’s exclusive search-distribution deals in 2025. At a computer-recycling stall, a worker offers $8 to rearrange a demonstration board. It claims to show competing routes. Every arrow leads to the same search box, including the one labeled somewhere else.
Check and save what the ruling changed → You read the ruling until your eyes ache and keep the relevant pages. The worker finally moves the alternative arrow somewhere alternative.
Rearrange the demonstration arrows for $8 → You earn $8 and enjoy making a second route work. Choosing it no longer requires ignoring the directions supplied by the first company.
Skip the display → You leave annoyed. The worker follows every arrow once more and ends at the same box with impressive consistency.
Scene: A worker presents a blank board whose loose arrows all point toward one unlettered search-box shape. Even an arrow pointing away loops back to the same search box.
Editable overlays: “SOMEWHERE ELSE” — Separate editable label beside the looping arrow
Source: Justice Department Wins Significant Remedies Against Google (2025-09-02)
ENC-S06-C · Please add a person
The U.S. Copyright Office says prompting alone does not make someone an AI image’s author. At a sign stall, a painter offers $8 to arrange cutout letters while she redraws a client’s generated design. The supposedly unnecessary human is now the urgent order.
Check and save the authorship distinction → You preserve the human-contribution distinction through tired eyes. The client’s instruction to make it brilliant remains different from making it brilliant.
Arrange the cutout letters for $8 → You earn $8 and enjoy the work. The painter makes actual creative decisions while the client searches for a shortcut to those.
Leave the stall → You leave annoyed. The client tries adding please to the prompt, hoping courtesy will supply the missing authorship.
Scene: A painter holds a brush above an unfinished blank design while loose unlettered cutout shapes await arrangement. The client’s tiny prompt slip sits atop an enormous stack of rejected blank generated layouts.
Source: Copyright Office Releases Part 2 of Artificial Intelligence Report (2025-01-29)
ENC-S07-A · Strategic small change
A roadside coin dealer reads Trump’s order reserving eligible forfeited bitcoin instead of selling it. He declares his till a strategic reserve, then offers $12 to move a heavy cabinet. Supplies for the collectors’ lunch are welcome. Suddenly assets need legs.
Donate supplies for the collectors’ lunch → You share supplies and gain a contact. The dealer unlocks the snack cupboard, the only reserve with a sensible withdrawal policy.
Move the cabinet for $12 → You strain your shoulders and earn $12. His assets remain strategically stationary; your payment immediately starts planning a fuel purchase.
Pass on the request → You leave disappointed. The dealer studies the cabinet, hoping a holding strategy will eventually move it across the room.
Scene: The proprietor stands beside a locked till and an unmoved heavy display cabinet, offering a moving job. A tiny locked cash drawer receives a grand velvet cover while the bulky cabinet blocks its owner’s path.
Source: Establishment of the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and United States Digital Asset Stockpile (2025-03-06)
ENC-S07-B · Please confirm where headquarters is going
A court blocked the administration’s FBI headquarters move to the Reagan Building in August 2026. At a freight shop, a clerk has stopped labeling his spare office cabinet. Moving it pays $12; lunch supplies are welcome. He would like one address that survives the afternoon.
Donate supplies to the freight crew → You share supplies and gain a contact. The clerk puts lunch on the cabinet, confident that its destination is currently within reach.
Move the cabinet for $12 → You earn $12 and sore shoulders, enjoying a move that requires only the clerk’s agreement and a clear patch of floor.
Pass on the offer → You leave disappointed. The clerk keeps the address label loose, the cheapest infrastructure contingency he can manage.
Scene: A clerk holds an unattached blank address label beside a stationary office cabinet and offers a moving job. Two forwarding arrows point toward each other on a box perched atop the immobile cabinet.
Source: Maryland Attorney General Statement on FBI Headquarters Ruling (2026-08-17)
Source: AP reporting on court blocking FBI headquarters move
Source: FBI: New FBI Headquarters in Washington, DC
ENC-S07-C · Both ways at once
Trump wanted daylight saving ended, then urged more evening daylight in April 2025. A clock repairer offers $12 to move a cabinet and welcomes lunch supplies. He has put one presidential position on each face. The clock disagrees with itself.
Donate some food to the repairer → You share food and gain a contact. He sets a lunch timer, a tiny clock policy everyone can support.
Move the clock cabinet for $12 → You earn $12 and sore shoulders, laughing as the cabinet finally moves forward without requiring a position on summer time.
Pass on the offer → You leave irritated. The repairer points both hands upward and waits for Washington to decide which direction counts as progress.
Scene: A repairer points to the opposing faces of an unmoved two-faced clock cabinet and offers a moving job. The two faces of the same cabinet clock show different positions of the hands; no digits appear in the artwork.
Source: AP: Trump Calls for More Daylight as Debate over Clock Changes Continues (2025-04-11)
ENC-S08-A · The summer permission slip
A fuel clerk has kept EPA’s 2025 emergency waiver allowing summer E15 sales. He invites you to inspect its temporary dates while selling some food for $5. The blend stayed the same. Its permission to exist beside a summer picnic required renewal.
Check and save the waiver’s limits → You save the temporary dates through tired eyes. The federal paperwork changes seasons more often than the fuel changes ingredients.
Buy some food for $5 → You buy some food. The clerk hands it over without requesting an emergency waiver for eating lunch during summer.
Skip the food and waiver → You leave annoyed. The clerk folds the expired notice beside the pump cover, two different ways of putting the same fuel away.
Scene: A clerk holds a saved blank waiver beside a rolled pump cover and unopened food for sale. A pump cover has a tiny calendar pinned to it like a garment waiting for its approved season.
Editable overlays: “2025 TEMPORARY E15 WAIVER” — Blank saved notice header
Source: Ahead of Summer Driving Season, EPA Allows Nationwide Year-Round E15 (2025-04-28)
